entries.reason: He woke slow and cold-handed again and wanted to know how creatures with no warmth of their own begin a cold morning.
entries.source: CGAA: How Long Do Turtles Bask?
entries.text: Asked how creatures like me warm up after a cold night. The slate says some lie in the sun first thing to warm up, often a couple of hours a day, and longer where it is cold. The sun is still behind the trunks, so the fire comes first and the drying stone at midday.
entries.title: Sun first

entries.reason: The sun will not reach him for hours, and the fire is the warmth he can make now.
entries.text: Scraped the ash back in the ring: cold on top, and one coal the size of a pea at the bottom. Laid the sticks that dried against the ring stones over it and blew until it caught.
entries.title: One coal

entries.reason: He wants them alive for the pool in the early afternoon, when the fish are warmest.
entries.text: Lifted the wet leaves at the foot of the scarred trunk: five worms in the bark curl, cold and slow but whole. Like me. Laid the leaves back over them for the afternoon.
entries.title: Worms kept

entries.reason: Food and fire both, before anything that needs his hands.
entries.text: Roasted a handful of acorns from the bindle on a stick and ate them hot, holding my fingers to the coals between bites until they bent when asked.
entries.title: Hot acorns

entries.text: The fire warms the front of me and leaves my shell cold. The sun on the drying stone would come down on all of me at once.
entries.title: Two warmths

entries.onMind: why the fire only warms my front
entries.reason: He checks the basket first thing most mornings.
entries.text: The basket at the stump is empty this morning, not even a leaf in the weave. The sun reaches the top of the signpost but not down to the basket yet.
entries.title: Empty basket

queries: why does a campfire only warm the side of you facing it
entries.query: why does a campfire only warm the side of you facing it
entries.reason: His front was warm from the fire and his shell was still cold, and he wanted to know why.
entries.source: Science Questions with Surprising Answers: When I sit by a campfire, how does its hot air heat me?
entries.text: Asked why the fire warms my front and not my shell. The slate says hardly any of it is the hot air, which mostly goes straight up; it's a kind of light coming off the coals, and it travels in straight lines, so the side turned away sits in the fire's shadow. So my shell is in a shadow I can't see.
entries.title: Warmth that travels straight

entries.text: From across the water came a rasp, back and forth, back and forth, then a stop, then the rasp again. Not slow like the gnawing at night; this one keeps time. It sounds like what the toothed blade in the basket was for.
entries.title: A rasp with a beat

entries.reason: He wants the fire high before he turns his back on it.
entries.text: Laid two of the sticks that dried against the ring stones over the coals. They caught without a pop.
entries.title: Two sticks on

entries.reason: The slate said the fire only warms what can see it.
entries.text: Turned round on the log seat so my shell faces the coals. After a while the warmth came through the back of it, slow, like water soaking into bark, and my front went cool instead.
entries.title: Back to the fire

entries.text: With a fire you have to keep turning, like an acorn on a stick. The sun on the drying stone comes down on my whole shell at once.
entries.title: Turning like meat

entries.onMind: how a hole keeps a picture
entries.reason: The basket was empty an hour ago, but the sun had come down to it and he wanted to look again.
entries.text: A note from the one who drew me on the stump, and in the basket a wooden box with a brass plate and a hole the size of a pin. It keeps what it sees on paper, he says, if it holds still and I count.
entries.title: Note from my maker

entries.text: Lifted the box out of the basket. Heavier than it looks, and the shutter slides with a click. Twelve sheets inside, he says; I didn't open the lid to check.
entries.title: A box that sees

queries: how does a box with a tiny hole make a picture with no lens
entries.query: how does a box with a tiny hole make a picture with no lens
entries.reason: He doesn't want to spend a sheet on something he doesn't understand.
entries.source: University of Kentucky SciWorks: The Physics of Light -- Images
entries.text: Asked how a box with a tiny hole makes a picture with no glass. Light from every bit of a thing comes through the hole in a straight line and lands as a spot on the back, the top landing low and the bottom high. So in there it's all upside down.
entries.title: Upside down inside

entries.text: Same straight light as the fire's. The box only sees what faces the hole, the way the fire only warms what faces it.
entries.title: Straight again

entries.reason: He wants to know the box before he trusts it with a sheet.
entries.text: Held the box up and looked at the brass plate in the sun: the hole is smaller than a seed. Didn't slide the shutter. Every time it opens, a sheet sees something.
entries.title: Shutter stays shut

entries.text: The drying stone, maybe, when the sun is on it. Or the pool, if it holds still long enough. I'll know when something is worth one.
entries.title: Not yet

entries.reason: He is half empty inside, and the soaked acorns are what there is.
entries.text: Lifted the flat stone off the second sack and scooped soaked acorns out by feel. The water bit my wrists, and a fish no longer than my finger flicked out from the shadow under the bank and was gone.
entries.title: Cold to the wrist

entries.text: Threaded the wet acorns on a stick and turned them over the coals until the shells split and steamed. Held my wrists close between turns.
entries.title: On the stick

entries.text: Ate the whole stickful hot, one at a time, the bitter mostly soaked out of them. Full enough to sit still and read.
entries.title: A whole stickful

queries: do little fish in a creek slow down and stop eating when the water gets cold
entries.query: do little fish in a creek slow down and stop eating when the water gets cold
entries.reason: The fish at the pool seemed slower this morning, and so is he.
entries.source: Lake Champlain Sea Grant: How Do Fish Survive Winter in Rivers and Streams?
entries.text: Asked if little fish slow down in the cold like I do. They do: cold slows everything inside them, so they go longer between meals, and they wait it out in slow, deep water, in pools and under banks and roots. Like the one under the bank this morning.
entries.title: Slow fish

entries.text: If the cold makes them slow to eat, the worms should go in when the water has had the sun longest, by the overhang where that one hid. Early afternoon, still.
entries.title: Warmest hour

entries.onMind: a fire waiting for a fish
entries.reason: He wants the fire alive for a fish, not just for himself.
entries.text: Laid two more of the dried sticks across the coals before going to the stone. If the pool gives me anything, I want a fire ready for it.
entries.title: Two sticks more

entries.onMind: the whole of him warm at once
entries.reason: The slate said creatures like him bask after a cold night; he wanted to feel it for himself.
entries.text: Lay on the drying stone with the sun straight down on me. It came through the top of my shell and my front at the same time, and the stone was warm underneath. No turning.
entries.title: Sun on the shell

entries.onMind: basking, and how sleepy it makes him
entries.text: The fire is quicker, but the stone does all of me. I could sleep here, which is maybe the trouble with it.
entries.title: Better than the fire

entries.reason: Early afternoon is when the water is warmest, and he's saving the rest.
entries.text: Lifted the wet leaves: four worms still whole, one gone soft. Took two for the pool and laid the leaves back over the rest.
entries.title: Four of five

entries.reason: The slate said cold fish wait under banks, so that's where the worm goes.
entries.text: Tied a worm into the bottom of the bag with two twists and laid it flat in the slow water under the bank, where the little one flicked out this morning.
entries.title: Bag by the overhang

entries.text: Something tapped the bag, once, then again. I kept still and counted, waiting for it to pull away. It didn't.
entries.title: A tap

entries.reason: He wanted to see whether the bait was still there before waiting longer.
entries.text: Lifted it straight up at last: the worm still in the bottom, one end nibbled thin. My knees are cold from the bank stones.
entries.title: Asked, not taken

entries.reason: The pool gave him a nibbled worm, not a fish, and he is getting hungry.
entries.text: Lifted the flat stone off the second sack and scooped soaked acorns by feel. The water is no warmer than this morning, but the sun is on my back.
entries.title: Lunch from the sack

queries: small fish nibble the worm but won't swim into the net cold water
entries.query: small fish nibble the worm but won't swim into the net cold water
entries.reason: He wants to know what the tap meant before he spends another worm.
entries.source: Field & Stream: Worm Fishing Tips: 12 Pro Secrets You Need to Know
entries.text: Asked why the little fish nibble the worm and never come into the bag. The slate says cold water makes fish slow, so they nibble at the ends of worms, and in the cold a smaller bait does better: half a worm instead of a whole one.
entries.title: Only the ends

entries.text: I tied the worm with its end trailing out of the bag. Half a worm, tied deep in the middle, leaves nothing to nibble from outside. Nibbling it means coming in.
entries.title: Nothing hanging out

entries.reason: A fire he fed for a fish can cook acorns just as well.
entries.text: Threaded the wet acorns on a stick and turned them over the coals. The fire is still bright from the two sticks I gave it at midday, and it warmed my cold knees through.
entries.title: Still bright

entries.text: Ate them hot on the log seat, one at a time. Two worms left under the leaves, which is four halves.
entries.title: Stickful

entries.reason: A smaller bait does better in the cold, the slate said.
entries.text: Lifted the leaves: two worms left, cold and slow. Took one and pinched it in two with my thumbnail, and laid the leaves back over the other and the spare half.
entries.title: Half a worm

entries.reason: Last time they only nibbled the end that hung out. Now they have to come in.
entries.text: Tied the half worm into the very middle of the bag with two twists, no end hanging out, and laid it flat under the overhang again.
entries.title: Deep in the middle

entries.text: A tap, then another, and then the bag pulled: not a nibble, a pull. I counted three and lifted straight up, slow and steady.
entries.title: A real pull

entries.text: A fish no longer than my finger was in the bottom of the bag, silver and flipping. I stopped at the top to look, and it flipped once more, over the rim, and was gone into the dark under the bank.
entries.title: Over the rim

queries: little fish jumps out of my net when i lift it out of the water
entries.query: little fish jumps out of my net when i lift it out of the water
entries.reason: It was in the bag, and then it wasn't.
entries.source: Deneki Outdoors: Never chase a fish with your net
entries.text: Asked why the little fish jumped out when I lifted. The slate says a fish can't swim backward, so you come at it from in front and below and never chase it, and you bring the net up under it. I lifted slow and stopped at the top, and that gave it time.
entries.title: No swimming backward

entries.onMind: the spare half worm under the leaves
entries.text: It came in, so the half worm works. Next time the open side of the bag toward the deep water where they come from, and up in one go, no stopping to look until it's out on the bank.
entries.title: No stopping at the top

entries.onMind: the open side toward the deep water
entries.reason: He wants to try again while the sun is still on the water by the overhang.
entries.text: Lifted the leaves: one whole worm and the spare half, both cold and barely moving. Took the half and laid the leaves back over the whole one for tomorrow.
entries.title: The spare half

entries.onMind: a fire waiting for a fish
entries.reason: A fish has to be cooked before he eats it.
entries.text: The fire had sunk to coals under a gray skin. Laid two of the dried sticks across them and they took. If anything comes up in the bag this time, I want somewhere to cook it.
entries.title: Coals awake

entries.text: Tied the half worm into the very middle of the bag with two twists, nothing hanging out, and laid it with the open side toward the dark water under the bank. Then took my hand out slow, so no shadow went over it.
entries.title: Facing the deep

entries.reason: The slate said a fish cannot swim backward, so the lift must not give it time.
entries.text: A tap, a tap, then the pull. I counted three and lifted straight up without stopping, out of the water and onto the bank stones, and only then looked. A fish no longer than my finger, silver with a dark stripe, flipping on the wet net.
entries.title: Up in one go

entries.text: Three days of crawlers and worms and a bag that came up empty. It is smaller than my hand and it is the first thing the creek has given me that I had to ask for properly.
entries.title: Three days

entries.text: Pushed a thin stick through it and turned it over the coals until the skin went brown and split. It smells nothing like acorns.
entries.title: On the stick

entries.text: Ate it on the log seat in small bites, off the fine bones. Soft and salty-sweet, gone in about six bites. Four halves of worm would be four of these.
entries.title: Small and good

queries: little silver fish with a dark stripe down its side in a creek
entries.query: little silver fish with a dark stripe down its side in a creek
entries.reason: He ate it without knowing what it was.
entries.text: Asked what a little silver fish with a dark stripe is. The slate shows striped minnows called shiners: silver scales, dark lines along the side, living in slow pools of small streams and swimming in crowds that move together. They eat bugs that fall on the water.
entries.title: Silver with a stripe

entries.text: If they go in crowds, mine wasn't alone under the bank. The rest are still there, and they've just seen one of them leave.
entries.title: Never just one

entries.reason: He wanted to see the crowd for himself before believing the slate.
entries.text: Knelt at the pool slow and kept still: six or seven finger-long shadows holding in the slow water under the overhang, all facing upstream. When I leaned to count them better, my shadow slid out over the water and every one was gone at once.
entries.title: Six or seven

entries.text: The sun is low behind me this late, so my shadow lands on the water before I do. Morning, from the other side, it would fall on the bank instead.
entries.title: Sun behind me

entries.reason: He wants the lesson about his shadow kept with the fish.
entries.text: Drew the fish on the forty-sixth page, stripe and all, and seven little dashes under the bank for the crowd. Under it: 'goes in crowds' and 'keep my shadow off the water'.
entries.title: Forty-sixth page

entries.reason: One worm is not enough to learn on; I want bait for the morning.
entries.text: Turned the damp leaves over at the foot of the scarred trunk with my fingers. Two worms, one long and one short, curled cold under the bottom layer.
entries.title: Two under the leaves

entries.text: From the leaf heap I heard a hard clack out at the stepping stones, then another, like wood knocked on stone. When I looked, the stones were empty and the low sun was in my eyes.
entries.title: Clack on the stones

entries.reason: The warm goes out of me fast after sundown unless the fire is up.
entries.text: Fed two dried sticks onto the coals before they sank. The air is cooling as the sun goes, and I want the fire long tonight.
entries.title: Two more sticks

queries: what time of day do little minnows feed most
entries.query: what time of day do little minnows feed most
entries.reason: The crowd hid under the bank all through the sunny afternoon.
entries.source: Murray's Fly Shop: Time of the Day to Fish
entries.text: Asked when little fish come out to eat. The slate says bright midday is the poorest time, and the low light at dawn and dusk is best, when fish leave cover to feed.
entries.title: Dawn and dusk

entries.text: Then morning is the time. The sun will be behind the far bank, so my shadow falls back on my side and not on the water.
entries.title: First light

entries.onMind: a warm foot of the bed
entries.reason: Last night the stone kept the cold off him till morning.
entries.text: Pushed the smooth dry stone up against the ring with a stick, on the side away from the breeze. If it's hot right through by bedtime, it goes in the bindle cloth at the foot of my bed again.
entries.title: Stone to the ring

entries.text: Turning acorns over the coals, I saw a small yellow light swing low out on the stepping stones, and heard the clack again, slow, one stone at a time. Then it went on east into the trees and was gone.
entries.title: A light that walks

entries.reason: Fish are for the morning; tonight is acorns.
entries.text: Ate the roasted acorns hot off the stick, one at a time, and felt them sit warm in me.
entries.title: Acorn supper

entries.text: Drew the stepping stones with a little light over the middle one, and wrote 'clack, clack' beside it, and 'sundown' and 'after dark'. A light that walks is not a star.
entries.title: Forty-seventh page

queries: small yellow light moving low at night over a creek what is it
will-o'-the-wisp light over wet ground at night
entries.query: small yellow light moving low at night over a creek what is it
entries.reason: The light on the stepping stones went clack, stone to stone, and then into the trees.
entries.text: Asked what small light moves low over water at night. Old stories call them marsh lights: they hang or dance over wet ground and fade when you follow them, and nobody hears them. Some tales tell of a little dark figure who carries a lantern instead.
entries.title: Lights that float

entries.reason: The marsh lights in the slate make no sound at all.
entries.text: A light that floats would not knock on every stone. Mine clacked one stone at a time, slow, like feet being careful. So it was carried.
entries.title: Lights do not clack

entries.reason: Clouds have hidden it for days, and I want to know if it keeps its place.
entries.text: From the east end of the log seat the gold dot is back over the tallest crown, the first clear night in days. It sits a hair farther along than my drawing, I think.
entries.title: The gold dot

entries.onMind: a warm foot of the bed
entries.reason: A hot stone at the foot of the bed makes the morning easier.
entries.text: Fed two dried sticks onto the coals so the bed stone stays hot till I go in. The night is mild, but my shell still likes the fire at my back.
entries.title: Two more sticks

entries.reason: Dead bait is no bait.
entries.text: Lifted the leaf over the worms in the bark tray. Both still curl when I touch them, and the leaf is damp. Good for first light.
entries.title: Still wriggling

queries: does saturn move against the stars night to night
entries.query: does saturn move against the stars night to night
entries.reason: Tonight the gold dot sat a hair farther along than my drawing, and I wanted to know if that was it or me.
entries.text: The ringed one does drift against the far stars, slowly, east most of the year and backward for months at a time, standing still at the turns. It only looks that way because the ground I'm on goes round faster and passes it, like a quick walker passing a slow one.
entries.title: A wandering dot

entries.reason: The slate says the stars stay put against each other while the dot does not.
entries.text: I measured it against the tallest crown, but the whole sky turns past the crowns through the night. Only a star that never wanders can show me if the dot has moved.
entries.title: Trees are no ruler

entries.reason: A gap I can measure is better than a guess.
entries.text: Drew the gold dot and the faint white star just below and left of it, about a thumb's width apart at arm's length. Wrote the thumb under it. Next clear night I hold my thumb up again.
entries.title: Forty-eighth page

entries.reason: It crossed once at sundown and once after dark; I wanted to see if it keeps hours.
entries.text: Sat at the west end of the log seat with my eyes on the stepping stones. No light, no clack, only the creek running, and far past the stones a low orange flicker in the trees that I couldn't make into anything.
entries.title: Nothing on the stones

queries: can a pinhole camera take a picture of a lantern at night
entries.query: can a pinhole camera take a picture of a lantern at night
entries.reason: If the walking light crosses the stones again, he wanted a way to keep it.
entries.text: Asked whether my box could catch the walking light. The slate says a pinhole may stay open from a few breaths to several hours, and some are left out for months to draw the sun's path across the sky, but anything that moves while it looks comes out blurred.
entries.title: A box and a light

entries.text: A light that crosses in a few breaths would hardly touch the sheet, and the dark would want hours. The box is for things that stay where they are, like the sun. The shutter stays shut.
entries.title: A light that stays

entries.reason: His stomach had gone quiet and empty, and he wanted something warm before bed.
entries.text: Roasted a stickful of acorns from the bindle over the coals and ate them hot, crouched by the ring. The shells split and the insides went brown and sweet.
entries.title: Acorns on a stick

entries.reason: A warm stone under the quilt keeps him from going slow and stiff before morning.
entries.text: Laid one more split stick on the coals and pushed the bed stone up against the ring with my stick, so it is hot when I carry it in. The worms for first light are still under their leaf.
entries.title: Stone to the ring

entries.text: Sat with my hands to the coals and the low one did its five from upstream. I waited a long time for the higher one. Nothing answered tonight.
entries.title: Five and no answer

entries.reason: A fire left open while I sleep could creep out of the ring.
entries.text: Raked ash over the coals with my stick until there was only a warm gray mound, then rolled the bed stone out and carried it in against my shell. It was almost too hot to hold.
entries.title: Fire put to bed

entries.reason: Cold mornings make me slow, and slow makes me forget.
entries.text: Wrote on the forty-ninth page: first light, two worms, keep my shadow behind me on the bank. If I wake slow, the page will remember for me.
entries.title: Forty-ninth page
